Put \(d=|\mathcal R|\).  On the fallback branch, \(\widehat\Gamma_N=((\lambda+\Lambda)/2)I\) is deterministic and
\[
 K_N=\{H:\lambda I\preceq H\preceq\Lambda I\}.
\]
Membership of \(P_X\) in \(\mathcal M\), through the spectral assumptions in \(\mathrm{def:fourier\text{-}model}\), then gives \(\Gamma\in K_N\) surely.  It therefore remains to consider the active branch, on which \(t_N\ge1\) and \(m_N\ge2\varepsilon_N\).

We first construct one simultaneous event.  If \(R\in[-1,1]\) and \(s\in\mathbb R\), convexity of the exponential on \([-1,1]\) gives
\[
 e^{sR}\le {1+R\over2}e^s+{1-R\over2}e^{-s}.
\]
After taking expectations and centering, the second derivative of the logarithm of the right-hand side is the variance of a random variable supported on \([-1,1]\), hence is at most one.  The logarithm and its first derivative vanish at zero after centering, so two integrations yield
\[
 \mathbb E e^{s(R-\mathbb ER)}\le e^{s^2/2}.
\]
Apply this bound to the real and imaginary parts of \(e^{it_Nu^\top X_k}\), which lie in \([-1,1]\).  Exponential Markov optimization and \(\mathrm{ass:iid}\) give
\[
 P_X^N\!\left(\left|\widehat\phi_N(t_Nu)-\phi_X(t_Nu)\right|>\varepsilon_N\right)
 \le4\exp\!\left(-{N\varepsilon_N^2\over4}\right)
 ={\alpha_N\over d}.
\]
Indeed, if a complex number has modulus greater than \(\varepsilon_N\), one of its real and imaginary parts has absolute value greater than \(\varepsilon_N/\sqrt2\).  A union bound over the finite set \(\mathcal R\) therefore gives an event
\[
 E_N=\bigcap_{u\in\mathcal R}
 \left\{\left|\widehat\phi_N(t_Nu)-\phi_X(t_Nu)\right|\le\varepsilon_N\right\}
\]
such that, uniformly over \(P_X\in\mathcal M\),
\[
 P_X^N(E_N)\ge1-\alpha_N. \tag{1}
\]

By \(\mathrm{ass:additive\text{-}decomposition}\) and independence,
\[
 |\phi_X(t_Nu)|=|\phi_U(t_Nu)|
 \exp\!\left(-{t_N^2\over2}u^\top\Gamma u\right). \tag{2}
\]
For \(u\in\mathcal R\), \(\|u\|_2^2\le2\).  The ray lower envelope, \(q_u\le Q\), and \(\Gamma\preceq\Lambda I\) consequently imply
\[
 |\phi_X(t_Nu)|
 \ge c(1+t_N)^{-q_u}e^{-\Lambda t_N^2}
 \ge c(1+t_N)^{-Q}e^{-\Lambda t_N^2}=m_N. \tag{3}
\]
On \(E_N\), equations (3) and \(m_N\ge2\varepsilon_N\) give
\[
 |\widehat\phi_N(t_Nu)|\ge m_N/2.
\]
Thus the modulus floor in \(z_u\) is inactive.  Both moduli belong to \([m_N/2,1]\), and the mean-value theorem for the real logarithm gives
\[
 \left|\log|\widehat\phi_N(t_Nu)|-\log|\phi_X(t_Nu)|\right|
 \le {2\varepsilon_N\over m_N}. \tag{4}
\]
Define
\[
 \ell_u=\log|\phi_U(t_Nu)|+q_u\log(1+t_N).
\]
The two ray-envelope assumptions give \(\log c\le\ell_u\le\log C\).  Taking logarithms in (2) gives
\[
 \log|\phi_X(t_Nu)|+q_u\log(1+t_N)
 =-{t_N^2\over2}u^\top\Gamma u+\ell_u. \tag{5}
\]
Substitution of (5) into the definition of \(z_u\), centering \(\ell_u\) at \((\log c+\log C)/2\), and using (4) prove simultaneously on \(E_N\) that
\[
 |z_u-u^\top\Gamma u|
 \le t_N^{-2}\left\{\log(C/c)+{4\varepsilon_N\over m_N}\right\}
 =w_N,
 \qquad u\in\mathcal R. \tag{6}
\]

Polarization of (6) yields
\[
 |(Z_N)_{ii}-\Gamma_{ii}|\le w_N,
 \qquad
 |(Z_N)_{ij}-\Gamma_{ij}|\le{3w_N\over2}\quad(i\ne j).
\]
For every symmetric matrix \(B\), \(\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\max_i\sum_j|B_{ij}|\).  Hence
\[
 \|Z_N-\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le {3p\over2}w_N=\Delta_N. \tag{7}
\]
For completeness, let \(\zeta\) be an eigenvalue of \(Z_N\).  The variational formulas for the smallest and largest quadratic forms imply that its distance from \([\lambda,\Lambda]\) is at most \(\|Z_N-\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\), because every eigenvalue of \(\Gamma\) lies in that interval.  Eigenvalue clipping preserves the eigenvectors of \(Z_N\), and therefore (7) gives
\[
 \|\widehat\Gamma_N-Z_N\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\Delta_N,
 \qquad
 \|\widehat\Gamma_N-\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\Delta_N. \tag{8}
\]
The spectral assumptions and (8) show that \(\Gamma\in K_N\) on \(E_N\).  Combining this fact with (1), and with sure inclusion on the fallback branch, proves
\[
 \inf_{P_X\in\mathcal M}P_X^N\{\Gamma\in K_N\}\ge1-\alpha_N
\]
for every \(N\), as well as all active-branch inequalities in the theorem.

It remains only to verify measurability.  The empirical characteristic function is continuous in the sample; modulus, maximum with the positive floor, logarithm, polarization, and eigenvalue clipping are Borel operations.  Thus \(Z_N\) and \(\widehat\Gamma_N\) are Borel measurable.  Let
\[
 \mathcal S=\{H:\lambda I\preceq H\preceq\Lambda I\}.
\]
This is compact and convex, and \(\widehat\Gamma_N\in\mathcal S\).  For fixed \(r=2\Delta_N\), define \(K(x)=\mathcal S\cap\{H:\|H-x\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le r\}\).  If \(x,x'\in\mathcal S\) and \(H\in K(x)\) is not in \(K(x')\), the point on the segment from \(x'\) to \(H\) at distance \(r\) from \(x'\) lies in \(K(x')\) and is at distance at most \(\|x-x'\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) from \(H\).  Interchanging \(x,x'\) proves
\[
 d_H(K(x),K(x'))\le\|x-x'\|_{\mathrm{op}}.
\]
Thus the active-branch compact-valued map is continuous in its center and hence measurable.  The branch conditions are deterministic, and the fallback map is constant.  This proves the asserted measurability.

Fix \(P_X\in\mathcal M\).  For \(J\in\mathcal J\), write \(S_J=D\cup J\).  We first prove the label-preserving bounds needed for the confidence intervals.  Let \(H,H'\) have spectra in \([\lambda,\Lambda]\), and put \(\delta=\|H-H'\|_{\mathrm{op}}\).

If \(Y\in S_J\), then
\[
 \gamma_{YT\cdot S_J}(H)
 =H_{YT}-H_{YS_J}H_{S_JS_J}^{-1}H_{S_JT}=0,
\]
because \(H_{YS_J}H_{S_JS_J}^{-1}\) is the row selecting coordinate \(Y\) from \(S_J\).  Also \(T\notin S_J\): members of \(D\) strictly precede \(T\), while members of \(J\subseteq A\) are incomparable with \(T\).  Positive definiteness makes \(\gamma_{TT\cdot S_J}(H)>0\), since it is the Schur complement of \(H_{S_JS_J}\).  Hence \(\beta_J(H)=0\), and similarly \(\beta_J(H')=0\).

Suppose now that \(Y\notin S_J\), and set \(B_J=S_J\cup\{T\}\).  By \(\mathrm{ass:distinct\text{-}targets}\), \(Y\notin B_J\).  Eliminating the coordinates in \(S_J\) from the block normal equations for regression of coordinate \(Y\) on \(B_J\) gives
\[
 \beta_J(H)=e_T^\top H_{B_JB_J}^{-1}H_{B_JY}. \tag{1}
\]
The denominator in the defining ratio is positive by the preceding Schur-complement argument, so this division is valid.  Principal-submatrix eigenvalues are bounded below by \(\lambda\), and coordinate restriction cannot increase operator norm.  Consequently
\[
 |\beta_J(H)|
 \le\|H_{B_JB_J}^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|H_{B_JY}\|_2
 \le{\Lambda\over\lambda}. \tag{2}
\]
Using
\[
 H_{B_JB_J}^{-1}-(H'_{B_JB_J})^{-1}
 =H_{B_JB_J}^{-1}(H'_{B_JB_J}-H_{B_JB_J})(H'_{B_JB_J})^{-1}
\]
in (1), together with \(\|H_{B_JY}-H'_{B_JY}\|_2\le\delta\), yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\beta_J(H)-\beta_J(H')|
 &\le\lambda^{-1}\delta+\lambda^{-2}\delta\,\Lambda\\
 &=\left(\lambda^{-1}+\Lambda\lambda^{-2}\right)\delta
 =L_\beta\delta. 
 \end{aligned} \tag{3}
\]
Equations (2)--(3) also hold when \(Y\in S_J\), because both coefficients then vanish.

On the fallback branch, (2), the exact representation in \(\mathrm{prop:ideal\text{-}fiber}\), and the fallback definition give
\[
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq)
 =\{\beta_J(\Gamma):J\in\mathcal J\}
 \subseteq[-\Lambda/\lambda,\Lambda/\lambda]=C_N. \tag{4}
\]
Thus coverage is certain on that branch.

On the active branch, let \(E_N\) be the simultaneous event proved in \(\mathrm{thm:fourier\text{-}region}\).  Uniformly over \(P_X\in\mathcal M\),
\[
 P_X^N(E_N)\ge1-\alpha_N,
 \qquad
 \|\widehat\Gamma_N-\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\Delta_N
 \quad\hbox{on }E_N. \tag{5}
\]
Spectral clipping puts \(\widehat\Gamma_N\) in the same spectral interval as \(\Gamma\).  Applying (3) to (5) gives, for every \(J\in\mathcal J\),
\[
 |\beta_J(\widehat\Gamma_N)-\beta_J(\Gamma)|
 \le2L_\beta\Delta_N. \tag{6}
\]
Equation (2) places \(\beta_J(\Gamma)\) in the fixed clipping interval, so (6) places it in the corresponding clipped interval in \(C_N\).  The ideal-fiber representation therefore gives
\[
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq)\subseteq C_N
 \quad\hbox{on }E_N. \tag{7}
\]
Since \(\alpha_N\le\alpha\), equations (4)--(7) prove, for every \(N\),
\[
 \inf_{P_X\in\mathcal M}P_X^N
 \{\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq)\subseteq C_N\}
 \ge1-\alpha_N\ge1-\alpha. \tag{8}
\]

Define the directed excess by \(\operatorname{ex}(A,B)=\sup_{a\in A}\inf_{b\in B}|a-b|\).  On \(E_N\), take \(x\in C_N\).  Some \(J\in\mathcal J\) satisfies
\[
 |x-\beta_J(\widehat\Gamma_N)|\le2L_\beta\Delta_N.
\]
Since \(\beta_J(\Gamma)\in\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq)\), equation (6) and the triangle inequality imply
\[
 \inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq)}|x-\theta|
 \le|x-\beta_J(\Gamma)|\le4L_\beta\Delta_N.
\]
Taking the supremum over \(x\) proves
\[
 \operatorname{ex}(C_N,\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq))
 \le4L_\beta\Delta_N. \tag{9}
\]
This argument matches branches by their ideal labels and never divides by a difference between effect values.  It therefore remains valid when distinct ideal branches collide exactly; the only division in (1) is protected by positive definiteness and the spectral floor.

Finally, every map \(H\mapsto\beta_J(H)\) is continuous on the spectrally bounded positive-definite set by (1) and continuity of inversion there.  The clipped interval for branch \(J\) has endpoints
\[
 \max\{-\Lambda/\lambda,\beta_J(\widehat\Gamma_N)-2L_\beta\Delta_N\},
 \qquad
 \min\{\Lambda/\lambda,\beta_J(\widehat\Gamma_N)+2L_\beta\Delta_N\},
\]
which are continuous functions of \(\widehat\Gamma_N\) and are correctly ordered by (2).  Since \(\mathcal J\) is finite and nonempty, the finite union is a measurable nonempty compact random set.  The fallback set is deterministic.  Thus all events and losses above are measurable.

We construct the two laws and verify all conditions, including the uniform derivative estimate.  Fix
\[
 m=6,\qquad \eta={1\over10},\qquad \kappa={1\over20},
\]
and define
\[
 f_0(x)=(1-\eta){e^{-\sqrt2|x|}\over\sqrt2}
       +\eta c_6(1+x^2)^{-6},
 \qquad c_6={256\over63\pi}.
\]
The gamma integral gives
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}(1+x^2)^{-6}\,dx
 ={\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(11/2)\over\Gamma(6)}={63\pi\over256},
\]
while the first summand is the standardized-Laplace density.  Thus \(f_0\) is an even probability density.  Applying the gamma representation of \((1+x^2)^{-6}\) and the Gaussian Fourier integral, followed by elementary half-integer gamma recursion, gives
\[
 \phi_0(t)={1-\eta\over1+t^2/2}+\eta e^{-|t|}P_5(|t|), \tag{1}
\]
where
\[
 P_5(z)=1+z+{4z^2\over9}+{z^3\over9}+{z^4\over63}+{z^5\over945}.
\]
Every coefficient is positive, so \(\phi_0(t)>0\).

Choose an even \(C^\infty\) function \(\chi:\mathbb R\to[0,1]\), equal to one on \([-1,1]\) and zero outside \([-2,2]\).  For \(M\ge1\), put
\[
 \delta=\kappa M^{-2},\qquad
 \phi_{1,M}(t)=\phi_0(t)
 \left[1+\chi(t/M)\{e^{-\delta t^2/2}-1\}\right]. \tag{2}
\]
Let \(\varphi_\delta\) be the centered Gaussian density of variance \(\delta\), and define
\[
 \widehat h_M(t)=\phi_0(t)\{1-\chi(t/M)\}
                 \{1-e^{-\delta t^2/2}\},
 \qquad f_{1,M}=f_0*\varphi_\delta+h_M. \tag{3}
\]
Equations (2)--(3) show directly that the Fourier transform of \(f_{1,M}\) is \(\phi_{1,M}\).

We prove positivity rather than assuming that (2) is a characteristic function.  Set
\[
 b_M(z)=M^2\phi_0(Mz)\{1-\chi(z)\}
             \{1-e^{-\kappa z^2/2}\}.
\]
Fourier inversion and the substitution \(t=Mz\) give
\[
 h_M(x)={1\over2\pi M}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-iMxz}b_M(z)\,dz. \tag{4}
\]
For every integer \(0\le j\le12\), there is \(B_j<\infty\), independent of \(M\ge1\), such that
\[
 \|b_M^{(j)}\|_1\le B_j. \tag{5}
\]
To verify (5), observe that \(1-\chi\) vanishes for \(|z|\le1\).  On \(|z|\ge1\), every \(0\le\ell\le12\) satisfies
\[
 \left|\partial_z^\ell{M^2\over1+M^2z^2/2}\right|
 =\left|\partial_z^\ell{2\over z^2+2M^{-2}}\right|
 \le C_\ell |z|^{-2-\ell}. \tag{6}
\]
By (1), each derivative of the Student Fourier term
\(M^2e^{-M|z|}P_5(M|z|)\), away from zero, is a finite sum bounded by terms of the form
\[
 M^{2+\ell+r}|z|^r e^{-M|z|}
 =|z|^{-2-\ell}(M|z|)^{2+\ell+r}e^{-M|z|}.
\]
Since \(M|z|\ge1\) and \(\sup_{y\ge1}y^ae^{-y}<\infty\) for every fixed \(a\), these are bounded by integrable multiples of \(|z|^{-2-\ell}\), uniformly in \(M\).  Derivatives of \(1-\chi\) are supported on \(1\le|z|\le2\), and every derivative of \(1-e^{-\kappa z^2/2}\) is bounded.  The product rule proves (5).

Using \(j=0\) in (5), and integrating (4) by parts twelve times using \(j=12\), yields a constant \(A_{12}\), independent of \(M\), for which
\[
 |h_M(x)|\le A_{12}M^{-1}(1+M|x|)^{-12}. \tag{7}
\]
For \(\delta\le1\), retain the Student component in the convolution and restrict the Gaussian variable to \([-1,1]\).  Since \(1+(x-z)^2\le3(1+x^2)\) there and \(\Pr\{|N(0,\delta)|\le1\}>1/3\),
\[
 (f_0*\varphi_\delta)(x)
 \ge a_6(1+x^2)^{-6},
 \qquad a_6=\eta c_6 3^{-7}>0. \tag{8}
\]
For \(M\ge1\), \((1+x^2)^6\le(1+M|x|)^{12}\).  Equations (7)--(8) imply
\[
 |h_M(x)|\le {A_{12}\over a_6M}(f_0*\varphi_\delta)(x).
\]
Thus \(f_{1,M}\ge0\) once \(M\ge2A_{12}/a_6\).  Also \(\widehat h_M(0)=0\), so it integrates to one; it is even and hence centered.

Equation (7) makes \(\int |x|^j|h_M(x)|\,dx\) finite for \(0\le j\le8\).  Because \(\widehat h_M\) vanishes on a neighborhood of zero, differentiation at zero gives
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}x^jh_M(x)\,dx=0,
 \qquad 0\le j\le8. \tag{9}
\]
If \(S_6\) has density \(c_6(1+x^2)^{-6}\), beta integration gives
\[
 \mathbb ES_6^{2j}
 ={\Gamma(j+1/2)\Gamma(11/2-j)\over
   \sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(11/2)},
 \qquad0\le j\le5.
\]
Combining this with the standardized-Laplace moments \((2j)!/2^j\) gives
\[
 \mu_2={41\over45},\qquad
 \mu_4={227\over42},\qquad
 \mu_6={17011\over210},\qquad
 \mu_8={204121\over90}. \tag{10}
\]
Let \(H_0\) have density \(f_0\), and let \(H_{1,M}\) have density \(f_{1,M}\).  By (9), the moments of \(H_{1,M}\) through order eight equal those of \(H_0+N(0,\delta)\).  Hence, for \(0\le\delta\le1\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb EH_{1,M}^8
 &=\mu_8+28\delta\mu_6+210\delta^2\mu_4
   +420\delta^3\mu_2+105\delta^4\\
 &\le {554293\over90}. 
 \end{aligned} \tag{11}
\]

The multiplier in brackets in (2) lies in \([e^{-2\kappa},1]\): on the support of \(\chi(t/M)\), \(|t|\le2M\), so \(e^{-\delta t^2/2}\ge e^{-2\kappa}\), while off that support the multiplier is one.  The positive rational summand in (1) therefore gives two-sided polynomial bounds of order \(|t|^{-2}\), with constants independent of large \(M\), for both \(\phi_0\) and \(\phi_{1,M}\).  If either scalar distribution had a Gaussian divisor of variance \(r>0\), the residual characteristic-function modulus would equal \(e^{rt^2/2}|\phi(t)|\), which diverges as \(|t|\to\infty\), contradicting its upper bound of one.  Both scalar sources are therefore Gaussian-indecomposable.

We next establish vanishing product divergence.  Fix \(v=1/10\) and let
\[
 q_{0,M}=f_0*\varphi_{v+\delta},\qquad
 q_{1,M}=f_{1,M}*\varphi_v,
 \qquad D_M=q_{1,M}-q_{0,M}.
\]
Their Fourier difference is
\[
 \widehat D_M(t)=e^{-vt^2/2}\phi_0(t)
 \{1-\chi(t/M)\}\{1-e^{-\delta t^2/2}\}, \tag{12}
\]
which vanishes on \([-M,M]\).  Retaining the Student component in \(q_{0,M}\), and restricting the Gaussian convolution variable to \([-1,1]\), gives a constant \(a_v>0\), uniform in \(0\le\delta\le\kappa\), such that
\[
 q_{0,M}(x)\ge a_v(1+x^2)^{-6}. \tag{13}
\]

The density \(f_0\) has a finite sixth absolute moment, so
\[
 \sup_t|\phi_0^{(\ell)}(t)|\le\mathbb E|H_0|^\ell<\infty,
 \qquad0\le\ell\le6. \tag{14}
\]
For \(r\ge1\), derivatives of \(1-\chi(t/M)\) are bounded by constants times \(M^{-r}\) and supported on \(M\le|t|\le2M\); its zeroth derivative vanishes on \(|t|\le M\).  Moreover,
\[
 \sup_{M\ge1,t\in\mathbb R}
 \left|\partial_t^r\{1-e^{-\kappa t^2/(2M^2)}\}\right|<\infty,
 \qquad0\le r\le6, \tag{15}
\]
because for \(r\ge1\) the derivative is \(M^{-r}\) times a fixed polynomial in \(t/M\) times a Gaussian, and the zeroth derivative is at most one.  Each derivative of \(e^{-vt^2/2}\) is a polynomial of degree at most its order times the same Gaussian.  The product rule applied to (12), using (14)--(15), therefore yields constants \(C_j\), independent of \(M\), such that
\[
 |\widehat D_M^{(j)}(t)|
 \le C_j(1+|t|)^j e^{-vt^2/2}\mathbf 1\{|t|\ge M\},
 \qquad0\le j\le6. \tag{16}
\]
In particular, all these derivatives belong to \(L^2(\mathbb R)\).

We justify the weighted Fourier identity used next.  Multiply \(\widehat D_M\) by smooth compactly supported cutoffs converging to one.  For each cutoff, differentiation under Fourier inversion gives \(\widehat{x^jD}=i^{-j}\widehat D^{(j)}\).  Parseval's identity \(\mathrm{lem:parseval\text{-}identity}\) and (16) make both the functions and their derivatives Cauchy in \(L^2\).  The limits agree with \(D_M\) and \(x^jD_M\) in distributions and hence almost everywhere.  Thus
\[
 \|x^jD_M\|_2^2={1\over2\pi}\|\widehat D_M^{(j)}\|_2^2,
 \qquad0\le j\le6. \tag{17}
\]
Expanding \((1+x^2)^6\) and using (17) gives the exact identity
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}(1+x^2)^6|D_M(x)|^2\,dx
 ={1\over2\pi}\sum_{j=0}^6{6\choose j}
 \|\widehat D_M^{(j)}\|_2^2. \tag{18}
\]
Repeated integration by parts in the one-dimensional Gaussian tail gives, uniformly for \(0\le j\le6\) and \(M\ge1\),
\[
 \int_{|t|\ge M}(1+|t|)^{2j}e^{-vt^2}\,dt
 \le C'_j(1+M)^{12}e^{-vM^2}. \tag{19}
\]
Equations (13), (16), (18), and (19) imply, for a constant \(A<\infty\) independent of \(M\),
\[
 \chi^2(q_{1,M},q_{0,M})
 =\int {D_M(x)^2\over q_{0,M}(x)}\,dx
 \le A(1+M)^{12}e^{-vM^2}. \tag{20}
\]
For product densities, direct multiplication and Fubini give
\[
 1+\chi^2(q_{1,M}^{\otimes N},q_{0,M}^{\otimes N})
 =\{1+\chi^2(q_{1,M},q_{0,M})\}^{N}. \tag{21}
\]
Choose \(M^2=30\log N\).  Since \(vM^2=3\log N\), (20) gives
\[
 N\chi^2(q_{1,M},q_{0,M})
 \le A N^{-2}(1+\sqrt{30\log N})^{12}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Equation (21) therefore tends to one.  Finally, Cauchy--Schwarz applied to the likelihood-ratio difference yields
\[
 \|q_{1,M}^{\otimes N}-q_{0,M}^{\otimes N}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le{1\over2}\sqrt{\chi^2(q_{1,M}^{\otimes N},q_{0,M}^{\otimes N})}
 \longrightarrow0. \tag{22}
\]

We embed this scalar experiment in three dimensions.  Set
\[
 a=(1,2/5,1)^\top,qquad
 \overline\Gamma=\Gamma_\star-vaa^\top.
\]
The successive leading principal minors of \(\overline\Gamma\) are
\[
 {9\over10},\qquad {189\over250},\qquad {294\over625},
\]
which are positive; elementary Gaussian elimination without row exchanges therefore gives \(\overline\Gamma\succ0\).  Apply to both scalar experiments the same Markov kernel \(z\mapsto az+G_{\overline\Gamma}\), independently across observations.  For any signed measure \(\nu\), integration of its kernel image against a function bounded by one is bounded by the total variation norm of \(\nu\); hence total variation contracts.  The image laws are, with labels chosen to match the theorem,
\[
 P_{0,N}=\mathcal L(aH_{1,M}+G_{\Gamma_\star}),
 \qquad
 P_{1,N}=\mathcal L(aH_0+G_{\Gamma_\star+\delta aa^\top}). \tag{23}
\]
They have convolution densities and are therefore Borel laws.  Equations (22)--(23) imply
\[
 \|P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}-P_{1,N}^{\otimes N}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 s_N=\delta={\kappa\over M^2}={1\over600\log N}. \tag{24}
\]

We now verify membership in the fixed class.  The successive leading principal minors of \(\Gamma_\star-I/10\) are
\[
 {9\over10},\qquad {13\over20},\qquad {8109\over25000},
\]
and those of \(4I-\Gamma(1)\) are
\[
 2,\qquad {126\over25},\qquad {44\over125}.
\]
The same elimination argument gives \(I/10\prec\Gamma_\star\) and \(\Gamma(1)\prec4I\).  Since \(s\mapsto\Gamma(s)\) is nondecreasing in Loewner order,
\[
 {1\over10}I\prec\Gamma(s)\prec4I,
 \qquad0\le s\le1. \tag{25}
\]

For a coordinate or pair-sum ray \(u\in\mathcal R\),
\[
 r:=|a^\top u|\in\left\{{2\over5},1,{7\over5},2\right\}.
\]
Direct comparison of the endpoint cases gives, for \(t\ge1\),
\[
 {1\over2}\le{(1+t)^2\over1+r^2t^2/2}\le{27\over2}. \tag{26}
\]
The rational component of (1) and the lower bound on the splice multiplier imply
\[
 (1+t)^2|\phi_U(tu)|
 \ge{9\over10}{1\over2}e^{-2\kappa}
 ={9\over20}e^{-1/10}>{2\over5}. \tag{27}
\]
For the upper bound, expand \((1+z)^2P_5(z)=\sum_kd_kz^k\).  Direct summation gives
\[
 \sum_kd_kk!={4714\over63}.
\]
Since \(e^{-z}z^k\le k!\) for \(z\ge0\), and \((1+t)^2\le(25/4)(1+rt)^2\) when \(r\ge2/5\), equations (1) and (26) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (1+t)^2|\phi_U(tu)|
 &\le {9\over10}{27\over2}
 +{1\over10}{25\over4}{4714\over63}\\
 &={37117\over630}<60.
 \end{aligned} \tag{28}
\]
The splice multiplier is at most one, so (28) applies to both source laws; evenness handles \(t\le-1\).  Thus every named ray obeys the common exponent-two envelopes with constants \(2/5\) and \(60\).

By (10)--(11), either scalar source used in (23) has eighth moment at most \(554293/90\).  If \(Z_3\sim N(0,I_3)\), radial Gaussian moments give \(\mathbb E\|Z_3\|^8=3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot9\).  Since \(\|a\|_2^2=54/25\), \(\|\Gamma^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\) by (25), and \((x+y)^8\le2^7(x^8+y^8)\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\|aH+G_\Gamma\|^8
 &\le2^7\left\{
 \left({54\over25}\right)^4{554293\over90}
 +4^4(3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot9)\right\}\\
 &<50000000. 
 \end{aligned} \tag{29}
\]
Normalize each scalar source by its positive standard deviation and multiply its loading by that standard deviation.  This leaves \(U=aH\), its ray characteristic functions, and the observed laws unchanged, while producing a unit-variance source.  Since its variance is at most \(41/45+1=86/45\), the adjusted one-column loading satisfies
\[
 \|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
 \le{54\over25}{86\over45}={516\over125}<9. \tag{30}
\]
It therefore has norm less than three and rank one.  Its first entry is positive, and the column-order convention is vacuous for one column.  Unit variance gives nonconstancy, and nonzero rescaling preserves Gaussian indecomposability.

For arbitrary \(u\in\mathbb R^3\), the source characteristic function is \(\phi_H(ta^\top u)\).  If \(a^\top u\ne0\), the two-sided polynomial bounds give \(\log|\phi_H(ta^\top u)|=O(\log|t|)\); if \(a^\top u=0\), it equals one.  Therefore each constructed law satisfies
\[
 -2t^{-2}\log|\phi_X(tu)|\longrightarrow u^\top\Gamma u. \tag{31}
\]
If \(\Delta\) is the covariance of any Gaussian convolution divisor of that law, its residual characteristic function has modulus at most one, so
\[
 e^{t^2u^\top\Delta u/2}|\phi_X(tu)|\le1.
\]
Taking logarithms, dividing by \(t^2/2\), and using (31) gives \(u^\top\Delta u\le u^\top\Gamma u\) for every \(u\), or \(\Delta\preceq\Gamma\).  The displayed \(\Gamma\) in (23) is itself a Gaussian divisor by construction, so it is the greatest one.

Finally, direct substitution into \(\Gamma(s)=\Gamma_\star+saa^\top\) gives
\[
 \Gamma_{WY}(s)-{\Gamma_{WT}(s)\Gamma_{TY}(s)\over\Gamma_{TT}(s)}=0,
 \qquad
 {\Gamma_{TY}(s)\over\Gamma_{TT}(s)}
 ={3/5+s\over1+s}=b(s). \tag{32}
\]
Under the partial order whose only relation is \(T\prec Y\), \(D=\varnothing\), \(A=\{W\}\), and the ideals are \(\varnothing\) and \(\{W\}\).  The first equality in (32) makes the ideal-edge collision product in \(\mathrm{prop:ideal\text{-}fiber}\) vanish, while the second gives the empty-ideal value.  Hence
\[
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(s),\preceq)=\{b(s)\},
 \qquad0\le s\le1. \tag{33}
\]
Equations (24)--(33), together with the additive independent construction (23), verify all spectral, envelope, moment, loading, rank, normalization, sign, order, greatest-divisor, and collision conditions.  Thus, for all sufficiently large \(N\),
\[
 P_{0,N},P_{1,N}\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{col}}\subseteq\mathcal M_\star.
\]
The inclusion \(\mathrm{prop:lower\text{-}class\text{-}sr\text{-}inclusion}\) also places both witnesses in \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{SR}}\).  This completes the construction.

Take \(P_X\in\mathcal M_\star\).  By \(\mathrm{def:lower\text{-}class}\), \(P_X\in\mathcal M\).  The representation in \(\mathrm{def:fourier\text{-}model}\) supplies
\[
 X=AH+G_\Gamma,qquad U=AH,qquad U\perp G_\Gamma,
\]
with \(1\le k\le p\), mutually independent nonconstant coordinates \(H_j\), \(\operatorname{Var}(H_j)=1\), \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=k\), lexicographically sorted loading columns, and no nondegenerate Gaussian convolution divisor for any \(H_j\).

Full column rank makes \(A^\top A\) invertible and provides the deterministic left inverse
\[
 L=(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top,qquad H=LU.
\]
Thus \(H\) is a measurable function of \(U\), and \(U\perp G_\Gamma\) implies \(H\perp G_\Gamma\).  Mutual independence and unit marginal variances give
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(H)=I_k.
\]
Finally, a nonconstant Gaussian coordinate has positive variance and can be expressed as the convolution of two centered Gaussians with positive variances summing to that variance.  It would therefore possess a nondegenerate Gaussian convolution divisor, contrary to the source assumption.  Hence every \(H_j\) is non-Gaussian.  These are exactly the defining observational conditions in \(\mathrm{def:sr\text{-}published\text{-}class}\).  Therefore \(P_X\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{SR}}\), proving
\[
 \mathcal M_\star\subseteq\mathcal M_{\mathrm{SR}}.
\]

By \(\mathrm{thm:smooth\text{-}splice\text{-}pair}\), for all sufficiently large \(N\), both witnesses lie in \(\mathcal M_\star\),
\[
 \tau_N:=\|P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}-P_{1,N}^{\otimes N}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow0,
\]
and their targets are
\[
 \Gamma_{0,N}=\Gamma(0),\quad \Gamma_{1,N}=\Gamma(s_N),
 \qquad
 \mathcal T_{0,N}=\{b(0)\},\quad \mathcal T_{1,N}=\{b(s_N)\}.
\]
By \(\mathrm{prop:lower\text{-}class\text{-}sr\text{-}inclusion}\), the same witnesses lie in \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{SR}}\), and they plainly lie in every superclass described in the theorem.  The stipulated target-map agreement ensures that their targets remain the displayed ones in every such class.

Because \(\Gamma(s)=\Gamma_\star+saa^\top\) and \(\|aa^\top\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|a\|_2^2=54/25\),
\[
 \delta_{\Gamma,N}:=\|\Gamma_{1,N}-\Gamma_{0,N}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 ={54\over25}s_N. \tag{1}
\]
For any \(\widetilde\Gamma_N\in\mathfrak E_{\Gamma,N}\), define
\[
 E_N=\left\{\|\widetilde\Gamma_N-\Gamma_{0,N}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 <{\delta_{\Gamma,N}\over2}\right\}.
\]
On \(E_N^c\), the loss under \(P_{0,N}\) is at least \(\delta_{\Gamma,N}/2\).  On \(E_N\), the triangle inequality makes the loss under \(P_{1,N}\) greater than \(\delta_{\Gamma,N}/2\).  From the definition of total variation,
\[
 P_{1,N}^{\otimes N}(E_N)
 \ge P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}(E_N)-\tau_N.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\mathbb E_{P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}}
   \|\widetilde\Gamma_N-\Gamma_{0,N}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 +\mathbb E_{P_{1,N}^{\otimes N}}
   \|\widetilde\Gamma_N-\Gamma_{1,N}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\\
 &\qquad\ge{\delta_{\Gamma,N}\over2}(1-\tau_N).
 \end{aligned}
\]
The larger risk is at least half this sum.  Hence every class \(\mathcal A\) containing the witnesses obeys
\[
 \inf_{\widetilde\Gamma_N\in\mathfrak E_{\Gamma,N}}
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal A}
 \mathbb E_{P^{\otimes N}}\|\widetilde\Gamma_N-\Gamma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \ge {\delta_{\Gamma,N}\over4}(1-\tau_N)
 ={27\over50}s_N(1-\tau_N). \tag{2}
\]
Since \(s_N=(600\log N)^{-1}\), this proves the covariance lower bound.

For the causal target, the singleton identities give
\[
 \delta_{\Theta,N}:=d_H(\mathcal T_{0,N},\mathcal T_{1,N})
 =|b(s_N)-b(0)|={2s_N\over5(1+s_N)}. \tag{3}
\]
For \(0<s_N\le1\),
\[
 {s_N\over5}\le\delta_{\Theta,N}\le{2s_N\over5}. \tag{4}
\]
Repeat the event argument in the metric space \((\mathcal K(\mathbb R),d_H)\), using the open ball of radius \(\delta_{\Theta,N}/2\) around \(\mathcal T_{0,N}\).  It gives
\[
 \inf_{\widetilde\Theta_N\in\mathfrak E_{\Theta,N}}
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal A}
 \mathbb E_{P^{\otimes N}}
 d_H\!\left(\widetilde\Theta_N,\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(P),\preceq)\right)
 \ge {\delta_{\Theta,N}\over4}(1-\tau_N)
 =\Omega((\log N)^{-1}). \tag{5}
\]
Thus covariance loss and causal-fiber loss are handled as distinct target metrics.

Finally, let \((S_N)\) be uniformly honest over such a class \(\mathcal A\), and put
\[
 h_N=\inf_{P\in\mathcal A}P^{\otimes N}
 \{\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(P),\preceq)\subseteq S_N\}.
\]
The honesty assumption says \(\liminf_Nh_N\ge1-\alpha\).  Define
\[
 r_N=\left[(1-\alpha)-\inf_{m\ge N}h_m\right]_++N^{-1}.
\]
Then \(r_N\to0\) and \(h_N\ge1-\alpha-r_N\).  Let
\[
 F_{0,N}=\{b(0)\in S_N\},\qquad F_{1,N}=\{b(s_N)\in S_N\}.
\]
These events are measurable: for fixed \(x\), the map \(K\mapsto\inf_{y\in K}|x-y|\) is one-Lipschitz in Hausdorff distance, and \(\{K:x\in K\}\) is its zero set.  Honesty at the two singleton targets gives
\[
 P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}(F_{0,N})\ge1-\alpha-r_N,
 \qquad
 P_{1,N}^{\otimes N}(F_{1,N})\ge1-\alpha-r_N.
\]
Total-variation transfer of the second event and the union bound yield
\[
 P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}(F_{0,N}\cap F_{1,N})
 \ge1-2\alpha-2r_N-\tau_N. \tag{6}
\]
On this intersection, \(S_N\) contains both points, so
\[
 \operatorname{diam}(S_N)\ge|b(s_N)-b(0)|.
\]
Taking the lower limit in (6), and using \(r_N,\tau_N\to0\), proves the honest-diameter assertion.  Equations (3)--(4) prove the displayed logarithmic order.  The proof used only membership of the two witnesses and agreement of the target maps on them, so it applies to \(\mathcal M_\star\), \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{SR}}\), and every stipulated superclass.  No upper bound over \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{SR}}\) has been invoked or asserted.

theorem.statement:
The answer is affirmative.  For every sufficiently large \(N\), there are Borel laws \(P_{0,N},P_{1,N}\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{col}}\subseteq\mathcal M_\star\) and
\[
 s_N=\frac{1}{600\log N}
\]
such that
\[
 \Gamma(P_{0,N})=\Gamma(0),\qquad
 \Gamma(P_{1,N})=\Gamma(s_N),\qquad
 \bigl\|P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}-P_{1,N}^{\otimes N}\bigr\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Each law has an everywhere positive scalar source density and a representation with one unit-variance, nonconstant, Gaussian-indecomposable source, a rank-one loading satisfying \(\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}<3\), the common ray bounds
\[
 \frac25(1+|t|)^{-2}\le |\phi_U(tu)|
 \le60(1+|t|)^{-2},
 \qquad u\in\mathcal R,\quad |t|\ge1,
\]
and \(\mathbb E\|X\|^8<50000000=M_8\).  Its displayed \(\Gamma(P_{j,N})\) is the greatest Gaussian-divisor covariance in every Euclidean direction.  Moreover,
\[
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(P_{0,N}),\preceq)=\{b(0)\},
 \qquad
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(P_{1,N}),\preceq)=\{b(s_N)\}.
\]
The laws may be constructed as common Markov images of scalar Gaussian-convolved densities \(q_{0,M}\) and \(q_{1,M}\).  If \(M=(30\log N)^{1/2}\) and \(D_M=q_{1,M}-q_{0,M}\), then a constant \(K_{\mathrm{wp}}<\infty\), independent of \(N\), satisfies the order-six weighted-Plancherel estimate
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}(1+x^2)^6|D_M(x)|^2\,dx
 =\frac1{2\pi}\sum_{j=0}^{6}\binom6j
   \bigl\|\widehat D_M^{(j)}\bigr\|_2^2
 \le K_{\mathrm{wp}}(1+M)^{12}e^{-M^2/10}.
\]
theorem.proof_tex:
Put
\[
 m=6,\qquad \eta=\frac1{10},\qquad \kappa=\frac1{20},
 \qquad c_6=\frac{256}{63\pi},
\]
and define the two symmetric densities
\[
 \ell(x)=\frac{e^{-\sqrt2|x|}}{\sqrt2},\qquad
 s_6(x)=c_6(1+x^2)^{-6}.
\]
The first density has variance one.  Beta integration gives
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}(1+x^2)^{-6}\,dx=\frac{63\pi}{256},
\]
so \(s_6\) is normalized.  Under the Fourier convention in
\(\mathrm{lem:parseval\text{-}identity}\), their characteristic functions are
\[
 \widehat\ell(t)=\frac1{1+t^2/2}
\]
and, writing \(z=|t|\),
\[
 \widehat s_6(t)=\psi_6(t)
 =e^{-z}\left(1+z+\frac{4z^2}{9}+\frac{z^3}{9}
                    +\frac{z^4}{63}+\frac{z^5}{945}\right).
\]
For completeness, the latter identity follows by substituting
\[
 (1+x^2)^{-6}=\frac1{\Gamma(6)}
 \int_0^\infty y^5e^{-y(1+x^2)}\,dy
\]
into the Fourier integral, applying Fubini's theorem (the resulting Gaussian-mixture integral is absolutely integrable), and repeatedly integrating the resulting half-integer gamma integral.  This gives the displayed polynomial.  In particular, every coefficient is positive and hence \(\psi_6(t)>0\).

Define
\[
 f_0=(1-\eta)\ell+\eta s_6,
 \qquad
 \phi_0(t)=\frac{1-\eta}{1+t^2/2}+\eta\psi_6(t).
\]
Thus \(f_0\) is an everywhere positive, symmetric probability density and
\(\phi_0(t)>0\) for every \(t\).

We next construct the splice and prove positivity rather than assuming positive definiteness of its multiplier.  Let
\[
 h(r)=\begin{cases}0,&r\le0,\\ e^{-1/r},&r>0,\end{cases}
\]
and let the even \(C^\infty\) cutoff be
\[
 \chi(z)=\frac{h(2-|z|)}{h(2-|z|)+h(|z|-1)}.
\]
Then \(0\le\chi\le1\), \(\chi=1\) on \([-1,1]\), and
\(\chi=0\) outside \([-2,2]\).  For \(M\ge1\), put
\[
 \delta=\frac{\kappa}{M^2},\qquad
 \phi_{1,M}(t)=\phi_0(t)
 \left[1+\chi(t/M)\{e^{-\delta t^2/2}-1\}\right].
\]
Let \(\varphi_\sigma\) denote the density of \(N(0,\sigma)\), with
\(\sigma\) denoting the variance, and define the signed inverse-Fourier correction
\[
 \widehat h_M(t)=\phi_0(t)\{1-\chi(t/M)\}
                  \{1-e^{-\delta t^2/2}\}.
\]
Then the inverse transform of \(\phi_{1,M}\) is
\[
 f_{1,M}=f_0*\varphi_\delta+h_M.
\]

We now obtain a uniform pointwise bound for \(h_M\).  Set
\[
 b_M(z)=M^2\phi_0(Mz)\{1-\chi(z)\}
                   \{1-e^{-\kappa z^2/2}\}.
\]
This function vanishes on \([-1,1]\).  For every integer \(0\le j\le12\),
there is a finite constant \(B_j\), independent of \(M\ge1\), such that
\[
 \|b_M^{(j)}\|_1\le B_j.                                      \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, on \(|z|\ge1\), differentiating the rational part of
\(M^2\phi_0(Mz)\) gives a bound \(K_j|z|^{-2-j}\).  For the Student part, each differentiated summand is bounded by a constant times
\[
 M^{2+j+r}|z|^r e^{-M|z|}
 =|z|^{-2-j}(M|z|)^{2+j+r}e^{-M|z|},
 \qquad 0\le r\le5.
\]
The last factor is uniformly bounded because \(M|z|\ge1\).  Derivatives of
\(\chi\) are supported where \(1\le|z|\le2\), and all derivatives of
\(1-e^{-\kappa z^2/2}\) grow at most polynomially times a Gaussian.  The product rule therefore gives an integrable upper bound for every derivative through order twelve, proving (1).

Since \(\widehat h_M(Mz)=M^{-2}b_M(z)\), Fourier inversion and twelve integrations by parts give, for a constant \(A_{12}<\infty\) independent of \(M\),
\[
 |h_M(x)|\le \frac{A_{12}}{M}(1+M|x|)^{-12}.                 \tag{2}
\]
More explicitly, the bounds without and with twelve integrations by parts are
\(B_0/(2\pi M)\) and
\(B_{12}/\{2\pi M(M|x|)^{12}\}\), respectively, so
\(A_{12}=2^{12}\max(B_0,B_{12})/(2\pi)\) suffices.

For \(0<\delta\le1\), retain only the Student component in the convolution and restrict the Gaussian integration variable to \([-1,1]\).  Since
\[
 1+(x-z)^2\le3(1+x^2),\qquad |z|\le1,
\]
and \(\Pr\{|N(0,1)|\le1\}>1/3\), monotonicity in the Gaussian variance gives
\[
 (f_0*\varphi_\delta)(x)
 \ge a_6(1+x^2)^{-6},
 \qquad a_6=\eta c_6 3^{-7}>0.                              \tag{3}
\]
For \(M\ge1\),
\[
 (1+x^2)^6\le(1+|x|)^{12}\le(1+M|x|)^{12}.
\]
Combining (2) and (3) yields
\[
 \frac{|h_M(x)|}{(f_0*\varphi_\delta)(x)}
 \le\frac{A_{12}}{a_6M}.
\]
Consequently, for
\[
 M\ge M_0:=\max\left\{1,\frac{2A_{12}}{a_6}\right\},
\]
the function \(f_{1,M}\) is at least one half of the strictly positive density
\(f_0*\varphi_\delta\), and is therefore everywhere positive.  Moreover,
\(\widehat h_M(0)=0\), so \(f_{1,M}\) integrates to one.  It is symmetric and hence centered.  This proves global density positivity.

The decay in (2) implies \(x^j h_M\in L^1(\mathbb R)\) for
\(0\le j\le8\).  Because \(\widehat h_M\) vanishes on a neighborhood of zero,
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}x^jh_M(x)\,dx=i^{-j}\widehat h_M^{(j)}(0)=0,
 \qquad 0\le j\le8.                                        \tag{4}
\]
For \(S_6\) with density \(s_6\), beta integration gives
\[
 \mathbb E S_6^{2j}
 =\frac{\Gamma(j+1/2)\Gamma(11/2-j)}
        {\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(11/2)},
 \qquad 0\le j\le5.
\]
Combining these moments with
\(\mathbb E L^{2j}=(2j)!/2^j\) for \(L\) with density \(\ell\), the even moments of \(f_0\) through order eight are
\[
 \mu_2=\frac{41}{45},\qquad
 \mu_4=\frac{227}{42},\qquad
 \mu_6=\frac{17011}{210},\qquad
 \mu_8=\frac{204121}{90}.                                  \tag{5}
\]
Equation (4) says that the moments of \(f_{1,M}\) through degree eight equal those of the convolution \(f_0*\varphi_\delta\).  Hence
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \int x^8 f_{1,M}(x)\,dx
 &=\mu_8+28\delta\mu_6+210\delta^2\mu_4
   +420\delta^3\mu_2+105\delta^4\\
 &\le\frac{554293}{90},\qquad 0\le\delta\le1.              \tag{6}
 \end{aligned}
\]

The splice multiplier obeys a uniform two-sided bound.  If \(\chi(t/M)\ne0\), then \(|t|\le2M\), so \(\delta t^2/2\le2\kappa\); outside that support the multiplier equals one.  Thus
\[
 e^{-2\kappa}\phi_0(t)\le\phi_{1,M}(t)\le\phi_0(t),
 \qquad t\in\mathbb R.                                     \tag{7}
\]
In particular, both characteristic functions are positive and bounded above and below by positive constant multiples of \(|t|^{-2}\) for all sufficiently large \(|t|\).  If either source had a Gaussian convolution divisor of variance \(r>0\), its residual characteristic function would have modulus
\[
 e^{rt^2/2}|\phi(t)|,
\]
which diverges as \(|t|\to\infty\), contradicting the fact that every characteristic function has modulus at most one.  Both sources are therefore Gaussian-indecomposable; their positive variances also make them nonconstant and hence non-Gaussian.

We next prove the claimed uniform Fourier-derivative estimate.  Fix
\(v=1/10\) and define
\[
 q_{0,M}=f_0*\varphi_{v+\delta},\qquad
 q_{1,M}=f_{1,M}*\varphi_v,
 \qquad D_M=q_{1,M}-q_{0,M}.
\]
Their Fourier difference is
\[
 \widehat D_M(t)=e^{-vt^2/2}\phi_0(t)
 \{1-\chi(t/M)\}\{1-e^{-\delta t^2/2}\}.                  \tag{8}
\]
It vanishes on \([-M,M]\).  Since \(v+\delta\le1\) for the values used below, the argument proving (3) also gives a constant \(a_v>0\), independent of \(M\), such that
\[
 q_{0,M}(x)\ge a_v(1+x^2)^{-6}.                             \tag{9}
\]

The law \(f_0\) has a finite sixth absolute moment, and consequently
\[
 \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|\phi_0^{(r)}(t)|
 \le\int |x|^r f_0(x)\,dx<\infty,
 \qquad 0\le r\le6.                                       \tag{10}
\]
For \(r\ge1\), the \(r\)-th derivative of \(1-\chi(t/M)\) is bounded by a constant times \(M^{-r}\) and is supported on
\(M\le|t|\le2M\).  Also
\[
 \partial_t^r\{1-e^{-\kappa t^2/(2M^2)}\}
 =M^{-r}F_r(t/M)
\]
for a bounded function \(F_r\), while the zeroth derivative has modulus at most one.  Finally, each derivative of \(e^{-vt^2/2}\) is a polynomial of degree at most the derivative order times that same Gaussian.  Applying the product rule to (8), and using (10), gives constants \(C_j<\infty\), independent of \(M\ge1\), such that
\[
 |\widehat D_M^{(j)}(t)|
 \le C_j(1+|t|)^j e^{-vt^2/2}
       \mathbf 1_{\{|t|\ge M\}},
 \qquad 0\le j\le6.                                      \tag{11}
\]

All functions in (11) are square integrable.  Approximate \(\widehat D_M\) in the Sobolev norms through order six by smooth compactly supported functions.  For each approximant, differentiation under Fourier inversion gives
\(\widehat{x^jD_M}=i^{-j}\widehat D_M^{(j)}\).  Passing to the
\(L^2\) limit and applying \(\mathrm{lem:parseval\text{-}identity}\) yields
\[
 \|x^jD_M\|_2^2
 =\frac1{2\pi}\|\widehat D_M^{(j)}\|_2^2,
 \qquad 0\le j\le6.                                      \tag{12}
\]
Expanding \((1+x^2)^6\) and applying (12) term by term gives the exact identity
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}(1+x^2)^6|D_M(x)|^2\,dx
 =\frac1{2\pi}\sum_{j=0}^{6}\binom6j
   \|\widehat D_M^{(j)}\|_2^2.                             \tag{13}
\]
For \(0\le j\le6\), repeated integration by parts in the Gaussian tail gives
\[
 \int_{|t|\ge M}(1+|t|)^{2j}e^{-vt^2}\,dt
 \le K_j(1+M)^{12}e^{-vM^2},\qquad M\ge1.                 \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, for integer \(r\ge1\),
\[
 \int_M^\infty t^re^{-vt^2}\,dt
 =\frac{M^{r-1}e^{-vM^2}}{2v}
  +\frac{r-1}{2v}\int_M^\infty t^{r-2}e^{-vt^2}\,dt,
\]
and iteration through \(r=12\), together with the analogous elementary bound for \(r=0\), proves (14).  Equations (11)--(14) imply, for a constant \(K_{\mathrm{wp}}<\infty\) independent of \(M\),
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}(1+x^2)^6|D_M(x)|^2\,dx
 \le K_{\mathrm{wp}}(1+M)^{12}e^{-vM^2}.                  \tag{15}
\]
The density lower bound (9) therefore yields, with
\(K_{\chi}=a_v^{-1}K_{\mathrm{wp}}\),
\[
 \chi^2(q_{1,M},q_{0,M})
 =\int\frac{|D_M(x)|^2}{q_{0,M}(x)}\,dx
 \le K_{\chi}(1+M)^{12}e^{-vM^2}.                        \tag{16}
\]

For product densities, Fubini's theorem gives the exact relation
\[
 1+\chi^2(q_{1,M}^{\otimes N},q_{0,M}^{\otimes N})
 =\{1+\chi^2(q_{1,M},q_{0,M})\}^{N}.                       \tag{17}
\]
Choose
\[
 M^2=30\log N.
\]
Then \(vM^2=3\log N\) and (16) gives
\[
 N\chi^2(q_{1,M},q_{0,M})
 \le K_{\chi}N^{-2}(1+\sqrt{30\log N})^{12}\longrightarrow0.
\]
It follows from (17) that the product chi-square divergence tends to zero.  Cauchy--Schwarz applied to the likelihood-ratio difference then gives
\[
 \|q_{1,M}^{\otimes N}-q_{0,M}^{\otimes N}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le\frac12\sqrt{\chi^2(q_{1,M}^{\otimes N},q_{0,M}^{\otimes N})}
 \longrightarrow0.                                        \tag{18}
\]
For this cutoff,
\[
 \delta=\frac{\kappa}{M^2}=\frac1{600\log N}=:s_N.        \tag{19}
\]

It remains to embed the scalar pair and verify every defining restriction of the fixed causal class.  In coordinates \((T,W,Y)\), let
\[
 a=(1,2/5,1)^\top,\qquad
 \overline\Gamma=\Gamma_\star-vaa^\top.
\]
The successive leading principal determinants of \(\overline\Gamma\) are
\[
 \frac9{10},\qquad \frac{189}{250},\qquad \frac{294}{625}.
\]
Successive completion of squares, equivalently the scalar-pivot
\(LDL^\top\) factorization, therefore shows \(\overline\Gamma\succ0\).
Apply to both scalar experiments the common Markov kernel
\[
 z\longmapsto az+G_{\overline\Gamma}.
\]
The image of \(q_{1,M}\) and the image of \(q_{0,M}\), respectively, are
\[
 P_{0,N}=\mathcal L(aH_{1,M}+G_{\Gamma_\star}),
 \qquad
 P_{1,N}=\mathcal L(aH_0+G_{\Gamma_\star+\delta aa^\top}),                \tag{20}
\]
where \(H_0\) has density \(f_0\) and \(H_{1,M}\) has density
\(f_{1,M}\).  They are Borel laws with smooth positive observed densities.
The variational definition of total variation shows that a common Markov kernel cannot increase total variation.  Applying this fact to the product kernel and using (18) proves
\[
 \|P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}-P_{1,N}^{\otimes N}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \longrightarrow0.                                        \tag{21}
\]

We first check the spectral restrictions.  The successive leading principal determinants of \(\Gamma_\star-I/10\) are
\[
 \frac9{10},\qquad \frac{13}{20},\qquad \frac{8109}{25000},
\]
whereas those of \(4I-\Gamma(1)\) are
\[
 2,\qquad \frac{126}{25},\qquad \frac{44}{125}.
\]
The same scalar-pivot factorization makes both matrices positive definite.
Since
\[
 \Gamma(s)-\frac1{10}I
 =\Gamma_\star-\frac1{10}I+saa^\top
\]
and
\[
 4I-\Gamma(s)=4I-\Gamma(1)+(1-s)aa^\top,
\]
we have
\[
 \frac1{10}I\prec\Gamma(s)\prec4I,
 \qquad 0\le s\le1.                                      \tag{22}
\]

For every coordinate or pair-sum ray \(u\in\mathcal R\),
\[
 r:=|a^\top u|\in\left\{\frac25,1,\frac75,2\right\}.
\]
For \(t\ge1\), direct comparison of the two quadratic polynomials gives
\[
 \frac12\le\frac{(1+t)^2}{1+r^2t^2/2}\le\frac{27}{2}.     \tag{23}
\]
For example, the lower inequality follows from
\(1+r^2t^2/2\le1+2t^2\), while at the smallest possible \(r=2/5\) the difference proving the upper inequality is
\[
 \frac{27}{2}\left(1+\frac{2t^2}{25}\right)-(1+t)^2
 =\frac{2}{25}\left(t-\frac{25}{2}\right)^2\ge0.
\]
The multiplier bound (7), the rational part of \(\phi_0\), and (23) give
\[
 (1+t)^2|\phi_U(tu)|
 \ge\frac9{20}e^{-1/10}>\frac25.                           \tag{24}
\]
For the upper bound, write
\[
 P_5(z)=1+z+\frac{4z^2}{9}+\frac{z^3}{9}
                    +\frac{z^4}{63}+\frac{z^5}{945}.
\]
If \((1+z)^2P_5(z)=\sum_kd_kz^k\), direct expansion gives
\[
 \sum_kd_kk!=\frac{4714}{63}.
\]
Because \(e^{-z}z^k\le k!\) for \(z\ge0\), and because
\((1+t)^2\le(25/4)(1+rt)^2\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (1+t)^2|\phi_U(tu)|
 &\le\frac9{10}\frac{27}{2}
 +\frac1{10}\frac{25}{4}\frac{4714}{63}\\
 &=\frac{37117}{630}<60.                                  \tag{25}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The splice multiplier is at most one, so (25) applies to both source laws; symmetry extends (24)--(25) to \(|t|\ge1\).  This proves the common exponent-two ray envelopes.

The scalar eighth-moment bound (6), \(\|a\|_2^2=54/25\), and (22) give a fixed observed eighth-moment bound.  Indeed, with \(Z_3\sim N(0,I_3)\),
\(\mathbb E\|Z_3\|^8=3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot9\), and
\((x+y)^8\le2^7(x^8+y^8)\) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\|aH+G_\Gamma\|^8
 &\le2^7\left\{
 \left(\frac{54}{25}\right)^4\frac{554293}{90}
 +4^4(3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot9)\right\}\\
 &=\frac{93995978093568}{1953125}<50000000.                \tag{26}
 \end{aligned}
\]

To impose the source normalization, replace either scalar source \(H\) by
\(H^\circ=H/\sigma_H\) and the loading \(a\) by \(A=a\sigma_H\).
This leaves \(U=aH=AH^\circ\), and hence the observational law and all ray bounds, unchanged.  Equations (4)--(5) give
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(H_0)=\frac{41}{45},\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(H_{1,M})=\frac{41}{45}+\delta\le\frac{86}{45}.
\]
Thus the single source has unit variance and
\[
 \|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
 \le\frac{54}{25}\frac{86}{45}
 =\frac{516}{125}<9.                                      \tag{27}
\]
The loading has rank one.  Its first entry in the displayed coordinate order is positive, and a one-column loading is already lexicographically ordered.  Nonconstancy and Gaussian indecomposability are preserved by the nonzero rescaling.

We now prove greatest-divisor status, rather than inferring it from the finitely many ray inequalities.  For an arbitrary \(u\in\mathbb R^3\),
\[
 \phi_X(tu)=\phi_H(ta^\top u)e^{-t^2u^\top\Gamma u/2}.
\]
If \(a^\top u\ne0\), the polynomial bounds following (7) give
\(\log|\phi_H(ta^\top u)|=O(\log|t|)\); if \(a^\top u=0\), that characteristic function equals one.  Hence, in every direction,
\[
 -\frac2{t^2}\log|\phi_X(tu)|\longrightarrow u^\top\Gamma u.             \tag{28}
\]
Suppose \(\Delta\) is the covariance of any Gaussian convolution divisor of the same observed law.  The residual characteristic function has modulus at most one, so
\[
 e^{t^2u^\top\Delta u/2}|\phi_X(tu)|\le1.
\]
Taking logarithms, dividing by \(t^2/2\), and using (28) yields
\(u^\top\Delta u\le u^\top\Gamma u\) for every \(u\).  Therefore
\(\Delta\preceq\Gamma\).  Since the \(\Gamma\) in (20) is itself the covariance of an independent Gaussian convolution factor, it is the greatest such covariance.

Finally, direct substitution in \(\Gamma(s)=\Gamma_\star+saa^\top\) gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Gamma_{TT}(s)=1+s,\qquad
 \Gamma_{TY}(s)=\frac35+s,\qquad
 \Gamma_{TW}(s)=\frac25(1+s),\\
 \Gamma_{WY}(s)=\frac25\left(\frac35+s\right),
 \end{gathered}
\]
and consequently
\[
 \gamma_{YW\cdot\{T\}}(\Gamma(s))
 =\Gamma_{YW}(s)-
   \frac{\Gamma_{YT}(s)\Gamma_{TW}(s)}{\Gamma_{TT}(s)}=0,                 \tag{29}
\]
while
\[
 \beta_{\varnothing}(\Gamma(s))
 =\frac{\Gamma_{YT}(s)}{\Gamma_{TT}(s)}
 =\frac{3/5+s}{1+s}=b(s).                                \tag{30}
\]
Under the strict partial order whose only ordered pair is \(T\prec Y\), the treatment-predecessor ideals are \(\varnothing\) and \(\{W\}\).  Equation (29) makes their sole edge product in
\(\mathrm{prop:ideal\text{-}fiber}\) vanish, and (30) gives their common value.  Hence
\[
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(s),\preceq)=\{b(s)\},
 \qquad 0\le s\le1.                                      \tag{31}
\]

Take \(N\) large enough that \(M=(30\log N)^{1/2}\ge M_0\) and
\(s_N\le1\).  Equations (20)--(31) verify, respectively, Borel existence, vanishing product total variation, the stated separation, spectral support, the common ray envelopes, the fixed eighth moment, unit-variance full-rank source membership, greatest-divisor status in all directions, and the exact singleton collision identities.  Therefore
\[
 P_{0,N},P_{1,N}\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{col}}\subseteq\mathcal M_\star,
\]
with the properties asserted in the theorem.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{Lap}}\).  Let
\[
 \mathcal I_4=\left\{r=(r_1,\ldots,r_p)\in\mathbb N_0^p:
 1\le |r|:=\sum_{i=1}^p r_i\le 4\right\}.
\]
Stars and bars gives
\(\lvert\mathcal I_4\rvert=\binom{p+4}{4}-1=d_4\), in agreement with
the definition of \(d_4\).  For \(r\in\mathcal I_4\), define
\[
 Z_r=\prod_{i=1}^p X_i^{r_i},\qquad
 \mu_r=\mathbb E_P Z_r,\qquad
 \overline Z_r=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N\prod_{i=1}^p X_{ni}^{r_i}.
\]
Put \(B=\sqrt{V_8}\), and let
\(\widehat\mu_r=\operatorname{clip}_{[-B,B]}(\overline Z_r)\), as
prescribed by \texttt{def:laplace-region}.  Since
\(\lvert Z_r\rvert\leq\lVert X\rVert^{|r|}\), the elementary inequality
\(z^{2|r|}\leq 1+z^8\) for \(z\geq0\) and \(1\leq |r|\leq4\), the
eighth-moment assumption \texttt{ass:eighth-moment}, and the definition
\(V_8=1+M_8\) imply
\[
 \mathbb E_P Z_r^2
 \leq \mathbb E_P\lVert X\rVert^{2|r|}
 \leq 1+\mathbb E_P\lVert X\rVert^8
 \leq 1+M_8=V_8.                                      \tag{1}
\]
By Cauchy--Schwarz, \(\lvert\mu_r\rvert\leq
(\mathbb E_PZ_r^2)^{1/2}\leq B\).  Projection onto the interval
\([-B,B]\) cannot increase distance from \(\mu_r\in[-B,B]\), and hence
\[
 \lvert\widehat\mu_r-\mu_r\rvert
 \leq\lvert\overline Z_r-\mu_r\rvert.                 \tag{2}
\]
The independent-sampling assumption \texttt{ass:iid} gives
\[
 \mathbb E_{P^{\otimes N}}(\overline Z_r-\mu_r)^2
 =\frac{\operatorname{Var}_P(Z_r)}{N}
 \leq\frac{V_8}{N}.                                    \tag{3}
\]
Summing (2)--(3) over the \(d_4\) indices yields
\[
 \mathbb E_{P^{\otimes N}}\lVert\widehat\mu-\mu\rVert_2^2
 \leq\frac{d_4V_8}{N}.                                 \tag{4}
\]
Consequently, Jensen's inequality and Markov's inequality applied to the
nonnegative random variable
\(\lVert\widehat\mu-\mu\rVert_2^2\), respectively, give
\[
 \mathbb E_{P^{\otimes N}}\lVert\widehat\mu-\mu\rVert_2
 \leq\sqrt{\frac{d_4V_8}{N}},                           \tag{5}
\]
and, using the declared definition
\(r_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}=\sqrt{d_4V_8/(N\alpha)}\),
\[
 P^{\otimes N}\!\left\{
 \lVert\widehat\mu-\mu\rVert_2>r_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}
 \right\}
 \leq
 \frac{d_4V_8/N}{(r_N^{\mathrm{Lap}})^2}
 =\alpha.                                               \tag{6}
\]

We next identify the population value of the reconstruction map.  The
centered standardized Laplace variable \(H_{\mathrm{Lap}}\) has density
\(h\mapsto 2^{-1/2}\exp(-\sqrt2\lvert h\rvert)\).  Symmetry gives
\(\mathbb EH_{\mathrm{Lap}}=0\), while direct integration using
\(\int_0^\infty h^m e^{-ah}\,dh=m!a^{-(m+1)}\) gives
\[
 \mathbb EH_{\mathrm{Lap}}^2
 =\sqrt2\frac{2!}{(\sqrt2)^3}=1,
 \qquad
 \mathbb EH_{\mathrm{Lap}}^4
 =\sqrt2\frac{4!}{(\sqrt2)^5}=6.                       \tag{7}
\]
Thus its fourth cumulant is \(6-3(1)^2=3\).
By \texttt{ass:laplace-source},
\(U=a^{\mathrm{Lap}}H_{\mathrm{Lap}}\).  Membership in the model in
\texttt{def:laplace-model} also retains the declared additive decomposition
\(X=U+G_{\Gamma(P)}\), in which \(U\) and the centered Gaussian vector are
independent.  Expanding the fourth joint cumulant by multilinearity, every
mixed term between the two independent summands is zero, and the fourth
joint cumulant of the Gaussian summand is zero.  Therefore (7) implies, for
every \(i\in V\),
\[
 \kappa_{TTTT}(X)=3(a_T^{\mathrm{Lap}})^4,
 \qquad
 \kappa_{iTTT}(X)=3a_i^{\mathrm{Lap}}(a_T^{\mathrm{Lap}})^3. \tag{8}
\]
The treatment-loading assumption \texttt{ass:treatment-loading} states
\(\lvert a_T^{\mathrm{Lap}}\rvert\geq a_{\min}>0\).  Hence
\(\kappa_{TTTT}(X)\geq3a_{\min}^4>(3/2)a_{\min}^4\), so the positive
floor in \(F_{p,M_8,a_{\min}}\) is inactive at \(\mu\) and every division
below has a strictly positive denominator.  The definitions of the
coordinates of \(a(\mu)\), followed by (8), give
\[
 a_T(\mu)=\lvert a_T^{\mathrm{Lap}}\rvert,
 \qquad
 a_i(\mu)
 =\frac{3a_i^{\mathrm{Lap}}(a_T^{\mathrm{Lap}})^3}
 {3\lvert a_T^{\mathrm{Lap}}\rvert^3}
 =\operatorname{sgn}(a_T^{\mathrm{Lap}})a_i^{\mathrm{Lap}}. \tag{9}
\]
In particular,
\[
 a(\mu)a(\mu)^\top
 =a^{\mathrm{Lap}}(a^{\mathrm{Lap}})^\top.              \tag{10}
\]
Independence in the additive model, centering, and the unit variance in (7)
also give
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}_P(X)
 =a^{\mathrm{Lap}}(a^{\mathrm{Lap}})^\top+\Gamma(P).    \tag{11}
\]
By (10)--(11), the matrix before spectral clipping in
\(F_{p,M_8,a_{\min}}(\mu)\) is \(\Gamma(P)\).  Assumptions
\texttt{ass:spectral-lower} and \texttt{ass:spectral-upper} put its spectrum
in \([\lambda,\Lambda]\), so clipping fixes it and
\[
 F_{p,M_8,a_{\min}}(\mu)=\Gamma(P).                     \tag{12}
\]

The construction in \texttt{def:laplace-region} is precisely
\(\widehat\Gamma_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}
=F_{p,M_8,a_{\min}}(\widehat\mu)\).  Both \(\mu\) and
\(\widehat\mu\) lie in
\([-\sqrt{V_8},\sqrt{V_8}]^{d_4}\).  The already established global
Lipschitz result \texttt{lem:laplace-global-lipschitz} and (12) thus imply,
pointwise in the sample,
\[
 \lVert\widehat\Gamma_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}-\Gamma(P)\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq C_{\mathrm{Lap}}\lVert\widehat\mu-\mu\rVert_2.   \tag{13}
\]
Combining (5) and (13), and then taking the supremum over the model, proves
the explicit uniform bound
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{Lap}}}
 \mathbb E_{P^{\otimes N}}
 \lVert\widehat\Gamma_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}-\Gamma(P)\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq C_{\mathrm{Lap}}\sqrt{\frac{d_4V_8}{N}}.          \tag{14}
\]
All quantities on the right are fixed model constants apart from \(N\), so
(14) is the first asserted uniform \(O(N^{-1/2})\) conclusion.  Notice that
no loading-norm bound has been used.

Spectral clipping puts \(\widehat\Gamma_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}\) in the same
spectral interval \([\lambda,\Lambda]\) as \(\Gamma(P)\).  Applying the
already established result \texttt{lem:fiber-lipschitz} to (13), followed by
(5), gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{Lap}}}
 \mathbb E_{P^{\otimes N}}
 d_H\!\left(
 \Theta_{TY}(\widehat\Gamma_N^{\mathrm{Lap}},\preceq),
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(P),\preceq)
 \right)\\
 &\hspace{18mm}\leq
 L_\beta C_{\mathrm{Lap}}\sqrt{\frac{d_4V_8}{N}}.
                                                               \tag{15}
 \end{aligned}
\]
This proves the second asserted uniform \(O(N^{-1/2})\) conclusion.

It remains to establish finite-sample whole-fiber coverage.  Define
\[
 \mathcal E_N=
 \left\{\lVert\widehat\mu-\mu\rVert_2
 \leq r_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}\right\},
 \qquad
 R_N=L_\beta C_{\mathrm{Lap}}r_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}.
\]
On \(\mathcal E_N\), (13) and \texttt{lem:fiber-lipschitz} imply
\[
 d_H\!\left(
 \Theta_{TY}(\widehat\Gamma_N^{\mathrm{Lap}},\preceq),
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(P),\preceq)
 \right)\leq R_N.                                      \tag{16}
\]
The exact representation in \texttt{prop:ideal-fiber}, applied once to each
of the two positive-definite matrices in (16), is
\[
 \Theta_{TY}(H,\preceq)=\{\beta_J(H):J\in\mathcal J\}. \tag{17}
\]
For any \(\theta\in\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(P),\preceq)\), the directed
true-to-estimated term in the Hausdorff bound (16), together with (17),
therefore supplies some \(J\in\mathcal J\) such that
\[
 \left\lvert
 \theta-\beta_J(\widehat\Gamma_N^{\mathrm{Lap}})
 \right\rvert\leq R_N.                                 \tag{18}
\]
This argument uses distance to the entire finite set and neither labels nor
matches its branches.  Thus (18) remains valid on exact effect-collision
strata, without any swap margin.

We verify that the terminal intersection with
\([-\Lambda/\lambda,\Lambda/\lambda]\) in
\(C_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}\) cannot remove a true effect.  Fix
\(J\in\mathcal J\) and put \(S=D\cup J\); by the definitions of \(D\),
\(A\), and \(\mathcal J\), one has \(T\notin S\).  If \(Y\in S\), the
definition of partial covariance gives
\(\gamma_{YT\mathbin{\cdot}S}(\Gamma(P))=0\).  If \(Y\notin S\), the
Schur complement of \(\Gamma(P)_{SS}\) is positive definite.  Cauchy--Schwarz
for that conditional covariance matrix gives
\[
 \left\lvert\gamma_{YT\mathbin{\cdot}S}(\Gamma(P))\right\rvert
 \leq
 \sqrt{
 \gamma_{YY\mathbin{\cdot}S}(\Gamma(P))
 \gamma_{TT\mathbin{\cdot}S}(\Gamma(P))}.
                                                               \tag{19}
\]
For any coefficient vector \(b\in\mathbb R^S\), let \(b_S\in\mathbb R^p\)
denote its extension by zero outside \(S\).  Because \(T\notin S\), the
spectral lower bound yields
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_P\!\left(X_T-b^\top X_S\right)
 \geq\lambda\lVert e_T-b_S\rVert_2^2
 \geq\lambda.
\]
Minimizing the left side over \(b\) is the Schur-complement variational
formula, and hence
\[
 \gamma_{TT\mathbin{\cdot}S}(\Gamma(P))\geq\lambda.     \tag{20}
\]
Choosing the zero predictor and using the spectral upper bound similarly
gives
\[
 \gamma_{YY\mathbin{\cdot}S}(\Gamma(P))
 \leq\Gamma(P)_{YY}\leq\Lambda.                         \tag{21}
\]
Equations (19)--(21), and the zero numerator in the case \(Y\in S\), imply
in all cases
\[
 \lvert\beta_J(\Gamma(P))\rvert
 \leq\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{\lambda}}
 \leq\frac{\Lambda}{\lambda},                          \tag{22}
\]
where the last inequality uses the declared strict bounds
\(0<\lambda<\Lambda\).  Thus every true element represented in (17) lies
inside the terminal clipping interval.  Combining (18), (22), and the
definition of \(C_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}\) in
\texttt{def:laplace-region} proves, on \(\mathcal E_N\),
\[
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(P),\preceq)\subseteq C_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}. \tag{23}
\]
By (6), \(P^{\otimes N}(\mathcal E_N)\geq1-\alpha\) for every
\(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{Lap}}\).  Taking the infimum in (23) therefore
gives
\[
 \inf_{P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{Lap}}}
 P^{\otimes N}\!\left\{
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(P),\preceq)\subseteq C_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}
 \right\}\geq1-\alpha                                  \tag{24}
\]
for every positive integer \(N\), which is the third assertion.

Finally, the construction is measurable.  Empirical raw moments are Borel
functions; coordinatewise interval projection, cumulant polynomials, the
maximum with a positive constant, the fourth root, and reciprocal powers on
the positive-floor domain are continuous.  Spectral projection is
continuous, and inversion is continuous on matrices bounded below by
\(\lambda I\).  The family \(\mathcal J\) is finite, so a finite union of
closed intervals with Borel endpoints, followed by intersection with a
fixed closed interval, is a measurable random compact set.  The same bound
as (22), applied to the spectrally clipped estimate, also shows that its
centers lie in the fixed interval, so this compact set is nonempty.  Hence
all estimators, events, and probabilities used above are well defined.
